findings.finding: Insights: f(n)=min lcm(x,y,z) with x+y+z=n. Minimal lcm occurs when two small numbers divide the largest c, giving lcm=c. So find smallest c such that n−c = a+b with distinct proper divisors a,b|c. Max a+b for given c is c/2+c/3=5c/6 (if 6|c). Hence c≥6n/11≈0.545n; achievable when 6|c and n=11c/6 (i.e. 11|n). For n=M+d (M=3^{2025!}), M is odd, huge, and 6∤M. Adjust by small d to meet divisibility. Compute f(M+d)≈⌈6(M+d)/11⌉ (or next feasible c). Then g(d)=⌊2025!·f(M+d)/M⌋/2025!≈f(M+d)/M truncated. Sum g’s → rational p/q; p+q mod 99991 needed. Pitfall: ensure c divisible by 6 and a,b distinct (c/2≠c/3). Use floor/ceil correctly for each offset.

Insights: Minimal N for sum n uses N+N/2+N/3 ⇒ N≥6n/11, equality when n≡0 mod 11 (N=6n/11). For n=M+c (M=3^{2025!}), M≫c, so f(M+c)=⌈6(M+c)/11⌉=6(M+c)/11 (since 11|2025!⇒11|M? actually M not, but 2025! factor matters later). Thus 2025!·f(M+c)/M = 2025!·6/11+tiny<1, floor =2025!·6/11 (integer because 11|2025!). Hence each g(c)=6/11, sum=36/11 ⇒ p+q=36+11=47. Pitfall: ensure 11|2025! so floor exact.

Insights: For N=M+c (M=3^K, K=2025!), smallest divisor >2 of N−1 is d: if c≡1(mod 3) →d=3; else if c≡0(mod 4) →d=4; else d=smallest odd prime divisor of c.  
f(N)=(N−1)(d−1)/d.  
For c≪M, g(c)=⌊2025!·(d−1)/d⌋/2025!; for c=0,4M extra “−1/2025!” term.  
Compute K=2025!; A_i=⌊K·(d−1)/d⌋ (minus 1 for c=0,4M).  
d’s: c=0→4; 4M→4; 1848374→11; 10162574→5081287; 265710644→4; 44636594→17.  
Sum A_i, reduce by gcd with K → p/q.  
(p+q) mod 99991 = 6825.   (Pitfall: handle large c=4M separately; ensure d from c, not N−1.)

Insights: For N, minimal x = N·uv/(uv+u+v) with distinct u,v≥2 (x = N/(1+1/u+1/v)). Smallest factor is 6/11 (u=2,v=3) if (uv+u+v)/gcd(uv,uv+u+v) divides N; next 4/7 (u=2,v=4). For N=M+c (M=3^{2025!}), test divisibility of N by D' (small) using M mod D' (3^K mod D'). Compute f(N) = N·uv/(uv+u+v) for the smallest admissible pair, then g(c)=⌊2025!·f(N)/M⌋/2025!. Sum six g(c), reduce fraction, find (p+q) mod 99991. Pitfall: assuming 1‑p‑x construction; need full uv/(uv+u+v) minimization.

Insights: f(N) = min X with 3 divisors a,b,c, sum N. Write a=X/m, b=X/n (m,n>1, m≠n). Then N=X(1+1/m+1/n)=X·D/(mn) ⇒ X=N·mn/D, D=mn+m+n. Need D/g|N where g=gcd(mn,m+n). Choose (m,n) giving smallest ratio R=mn/D, subject to T:=D/g dividing N. For N=M=3^{2025!}, only T that are powers of 3 work; best pair (3,6) gives T=3, R=2/3 ⇒ f(M)=2M/3. For N=M+c (c even), N≡c+1 (mod p) for any odd p≤2025 (since 3^{2025!}≡1). So smallest odd prime divisor of N−1 is smallest odd prime factor of c. Use pair (m,n) with T dividing N (i.e., T|c+1). Compute g(c)=⌊2025!·R⌋/2025! for each c, sum, reduce p/q, output (p+q) mod 99991. Pitfalls: ensure X integer (T|N), handle c=0 (use (3,6)), c=4M (N=5M, treat similarly). Use CRT for M mod T when T has factor 3.

Insights: For N=M+c (M=3^{2025!}), smallest x comes from divisors u<v≥2 with x=N·uv/(uv+u+v). Need D=uv+u+v, g=gcd(uv,D); let B=D/g. N must be multiple of m=B·lcm(g/ gcd(u,g), g/ gcd(v,g)). Test small (u,v) pairs: (2,3) → m=11 (needs N≡0 mod11); (2,4) → m=7; (2,5) → m=17; (2,6) → m=10; (3,4) → m=19, etc. Compute N mod each m using M≡1 (mod any m not dividing 3) and c values. For given c’s, only (2,5) works for c2 (N≡0 mod5? actually N≡0 mod5 gives m=5? but need extra factor → m=10 fails). After checking, the minimal feasible pair for each N yields:
c0: (2,4) → x=3N/4 → g(0)=3/4−1/2025!
c1 (4M): same → g=15/4−1/2025!
c2 (1848374): smallest m=11 fails, next m=7 fails, m=5 fails (needs N≡0 mod10), m=17 fails → use trivial 1+p+N → p=largest divisor< N/2 → p= (N−1)/11 → d=11 → g=10/11.
c3 (10162574): N≡0 mod5 → pair (2,6) needs N≡0 mod10 → fails; next viable (2,5) needs N≡0 mod17 → fails; use p from N−1 → d=5081287 → g=⌊2025!·(d−1)/d⌋/2025!.
c4 (265710644): N≡0 mod4 → d=4 → g=3/4.
c5 (44636594): N−1 smallest odd divisor=17 → g=16/17.
Sum A_i = (2025!·3/4−1)+(2025!·15/4−1)+(2025!·10/11)+(2025!·5081286//5081287)+(2025!·3/4)+(2025!·16/17). Reduce fraction → p+q≡6825 (mod 99991).

Insights: n odd ⇒ use divisors {1,2,x} (x=n‑3) or better {2,d,x} where d|n‑2, d odd. Smallest odd prime p dividing n‑2 (or q dividing n‑1) gives minimal x≈(p‑1)/p·(n‑2) or (q‑1)/q·(n‑1). For M=3^{2025!}, n=M+c (c even). Small c ⇒ p,q are tiny (from c‑1,c). Hence f<M ⇒ K=2025!‑1. For c=4M, p,q>2025 ⇒ f>M ⇒ K=2025!. Sum K=6·2025!‑5 ⇒ reduced fraction (6·2025!‑5)/2025! → (7·2025!/5)‑1. Compute 2025! mod 99991 =57239, inv5=79993 ⇒ answer (7·57239·inv5‑1) mod 99991 =20139.

Insights: Minimal x uses three divisors x/u, x/v, x with u<v≥2. Factor λ=uv/(uv+u+v). Feasibility: N must be divisible by m=B·L where B=(uv+u+v)/g, L=lcm(g/gcd(u,g),g/gcd(v,g)), g=gcd(uv,uv+u+v). For each N=M+c (M=3^{2025!}), test small (u,v) (≤30) to find smallest λ with N≡0 (mod m). Compute g(c)=⌊2025!·λ·(1+c/M)⌋/2025!. Sum six g’s, reduce p/q, output (p+q) mod 99991. Pitfalls: assuming 1‑p‑x triple gives minimal x (false); must enforce extra divisibility L; handle c=4M (N=5M) separately.

Insights: For N=M+c (M=3^{2025!}), minimal x comes from either {1,a,x} with a=(N‑1)/q (q=smallest odd prime divisor of N‑1) giving x≈(q‑1)/q·N, or from {2,d,x} with d=(N‑2)/p (p=smallest odd prime divisor of N‑2) giving x≈(p‑1)/p·N. For all small c, q or p ≤2025, so x<N and x<M ⇒ f(N)<M ⇒ floor term =2025!‑1. For c=4M, N=5M, no small divisor, but {1,2,x} gives f≈N‑3> M ⇒ term =2025!. Sum of six terms =6·2025!‑5 ⇒ reduced to (7·2025!/5)‑1. Compute 2025! mod 99991 =57239, inv5=79993 ⇒ (7·57239·inv5‑1) mod 99991 =20139. Answer: 20139.
